**Vignette: Marcus, Age 29**

Marcus grew up in a small coastal town in southern France, the kind of place where summers stretched long and the sea felt like a permanent fixture of safety. He was twenty-six when the floods came. A slow-moving storm system stalled over the region for three days, and by the time the rivers breached their banks, the water rose faster than anyone had anticipated. Marcus was trapped in his apartment for nearly eighteen hours, watching the waterline climb the walls of the ground floor, unable to reach his mother by phone, certain at several points during the night that he was going to drown. He was eventually evacuated by boat, cold and shaking, to a temporary shelter in a school gymnasium. His apartment was destroyed. Several people in his neighborhood did not survive.

In the weeks that followed, Marcus threw himself into the practical work of rebuilding — filing insurance claims, staying with a cousin in Lyon, replacing what he had lost. He told himself he was fine. He was alive. He kept moving.

He relocated to Lyon permanently and found work as a salesperson for a medical equipment company, a role that suits his natural ease with people. On the surface, Marcus is good at his job. He is warm, articulate, and capable of holding a conversation with almost anyone. His colleagues see someone who is sociable and driven. What they do not see is that he checks the weather application on his phone between eight and twelve times a day. On mornings when the forecast shows rain, he wakes with a tightness in his chest that he cannot fully explain and sometimes calls in sick rather than face the drive to work in wet conditions. During a client meeting last spring, a burst pipe in the building's ceiling sent water sheeting across the floor, and Marcus left the room abruptly without explanation. He sat in his car for forty minutes before he could drive.

At night, sleep is unreliable. He frequently wakes between two and four in the morning with his heart pounding, the sensation of cold water vivid and immediate, the darkness of his old apartment pressing in around him. He does not always remember a specific dream — sometimes it is simply the feeling of being submerged, of helplessness so complete it has no edges. He lies awake afterward, listening to the sounds of the building, reassuring himself of where he is.

Marcus has not returned to the coast. He tells people he simply prefers the city now, and he has rehearsed this explanation so many times it has begun to feel true. In reality, the thought of standing near open water produces a physical response he finds humiliating — a rushing in his ears, a sudden and irrational certainty that the ground beneath him is not stable. He declined a colleague's wedding invitation last summer when he learned it was to be held at a lakeside venue. He said he had a prior commitment.

What troubles Marcus most is the sense that he has become a diminished version of himself. He used to be someone who went sailing with friends, who found the sea calming. Now he cannot watch a film with flood imagery without leaving the room. He notices himself scanning environments for exits, calculating how quickly a space could fill with water. He knows, on some rational level, that this is not useful thinking. He cannot stop doing it.

He has mentioned none of this to anyone. He is twenty-nine, single, and has built a life that looks, from the outside, entirely intact. The version of himself that nearly drowned in a ground-floor apartment three years ago is not someone he has introduced to the people in his current life. He carries that night the way he carries his phone — constantly, and close to his body, checking it more often than he would like to admit.
